title: Orbital-Induced Peierls Transitions: How Orbitals Orchestrate Lattice Instability
abstract: The Peierls transition is typically regarded as a phenomenon inherent to one-dimensional (1D) materials. However, orbital degrees of freedom can induce this instability even in higher dimensions. Two mechanisms are primarily responsible. First, the anisotropic shape of $p$ and $d$ orbitals can lead to effective "1D-zation" of the electronic spectrum. Second, orbital degrees of freedom can lift band degeneracy by shifting bands relative to each other via the local or band Jahn-Teller effect, thereby affecting the nesting of the Fermi surface. The orbital-induced Peierls effect is most commonly observed when ligand octahedra surrounding transition metals share edges, and less frequently in face-sharing geometries. In this review, we discuss the underlying physical mechanisms, the materials in which this phenomenon occurs, the characteristics of the high-temperature undistorted phase, and the role of local effects such as the formation of molecular orbitals.
summary: This review explores how orbital degrees of freedom can drive lattice instabilities, such as the Peierls transition, even in higher-dimensional materials. It details two key mechanisms: orbital anisotropy leading to effective 1D behavior, and the Jahn-Teller effect lifting band degeneracies. The work is crucial for understanding structural transitions in transition metal oxides based on orbital interactions.
main_problem: The paper investigates how orbital degrees of freedom can induce the Peierls transition (lattice instability) in higher dimensions, moving beyond the traditional one-dimensional context.
main_result: Orbital anisotropy allows the Peierls instability to manifest in higher dimensions, often synergistically coupled with the Jahn-Teller effect in edge-sharing transition metal oxide structures.
method: The analysis uses theoretical concepts like the generalized susceptibility ($\chi_0(\vec{q})$) and compares energy gains from electronic structure changes (e.g., molecular orbital formation) against elastic energy loss.
model_or_system: The focus is on transition metal compounds, particularly those with partially filled $t_{2g}$ orbitals, often exhibiting edge-sharing octahedral geometries (e.g., in spinels).
key_observables: Gap opening at specific wavevectors, divergence of the generalized susceptibility, and band structure evolution under Jahn-Teller distortions.
important_parameters: Orbital filling ($d^n$), lattice geometry (edge-sharing vs. face-sharing), and the strength of orbital anisotropy.
main_assumptions: The review primarily focuses on $d$ orbitals and notes the difficulty in cleanly separating the energy contributions from the band Jahn-Teller effect versus the Peierls mechanism.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the Peierls transition in 1D chains, compare orbital sharing in different octahedral geometries, and show $t_{2g}$ band dispersions under structural distortions in spinel structures.
paper_structure: The review progresses from the traditional 1D Peierls concept to mechanisms allowing instability in higher dimensions, detailing the role of orbital anisotropy and Jahn-Teller coupling in specific crystal structures.
why_interesting: The coupling between orbital physics, lattice instability (Peierls), and electronic correlations is a cornerstone of strongly correlated electron physics, relevant to understanding Mott insulators and metal-insulator transitions.
